title: Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney

concept.text: The innovation would enable an adult human’s own kidney to acquire additional working nephrons: the microscopic units that filter blood and process the resulting fluid into urine. New nephrons would need to connect to the circulation, perform coordinated filtration and tubular processing, and drain into the kidney’s collecting system. The target is an increase in nephron number that meaningfully improves kidney function, rather than the appearance of isolated nephron-like structures.

Developmental nephron formation ends around birth in mammals, with timing varying by species. Repair of cells within an existing nephron is biologically different from constructing an additional whole nephron. A January 2022 review describes repair of injured tubular epithelium but reports no evidence of new nephron generation within a postnatal mammalian kidney and no postnatal progenitor capable of producing an entire nephron. Inducing that developmental capability within an adult human’s native kidney is the proposed advance.

significance.text: Restoring nephron number would offer a way to recover renal function within the existing organ. After developmental nephrogenesis ends, repairing surviving cells does not itself replace lost whole nephrons. If enough new nephrons could be integrated and kept functional, the treatment could expand the kidney’s working capacity beyond what repair or preservation of its remaining structures can accomplish.

Conditional clinical significance: severe progressive chronic kidney disease can lead to dialysis or transplantation, although that progression is not inevitable for every patient. Sufficient, sustained restoration of native kidney function could allow some patients to avoid or stop dialysis without receiving a transplanted organ, potentially including people who cannot obtain a transplant. That outcome would depend on the amount and quality of recovered renal function. A rise in filtration alone would not establish adequate overall kidney function, durable benefit, or dialysis independence.

Impact limits and synthesis: benefit would have to be demonstrated in diseased kidneys, where the conditions that caused nephron loss may persist. Creating additional nephrons would not by itself establish that the underlying disease had been controlled. Success would also provide no automatic basis for expecting regeneration of limbs, spinal cord circuitry, or heart muscle; those tissues require different structures, connections, and functional demonstrations.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is controlled formation of complete new nephrons within an adult native kidney, followed by their productive integration into a functioning organ. The January 2022 review identifies the absence of a postnatal pan-nephron progenitor as a fundamental obstacle. A treatment would therefore need to establish an appropriate nephron-forming program, potentially through developmental reprogramming or introduced cells, rather than relying on the repair response of existing tubular cells.

Cell identity is only one barrier. Newly generated tissue would need appropriately organized glomerular and tubular components, a blood supply that supports filtration, and open connections through which urinary filtrate can leave. The review explicitly identifies sufficient nephron quantity and patent urinary drainage as requirements for renal replacement using transplanted tissue. Applying those requirements to regeneration inside the native kidney is a reasoned engineering extension: new filtering structures would contribute little useful replacement function if their filtrate could not drain.

The program would also have to produce suitable mature cell types without disrupting the function that the kidney still retains. The review treats productive versus disruptive in situ reprogramming as an unresolved issue. It also states that the number of functional nephrons needed for clinically useful renal replacement remains uncertain. Consequently, the supplied evidence does not justify a fixed nephron-count target or establish how many newly formed units would deliver a particular clinical benefit.

Engineering synthesis: a practical therapy would need to control where regeneration occurs, how much tissue forms, and when the developmental program stops. It would also need to function in a damaged adult organ and preserve the added nephrons over time. These are necessary development questions, not capabilities shown to have been solved in the supplied evidence.

current_state.text: The historical scientific baseline is Melissa H. Little and Benjamin D. Humphreys’ review, “Regrow or Repair: An Update on Potential Regenerative Therapies for the Kidney,” published in January 2022 in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, volume 33, pages 15–32, DOI 10.1681/ASN.2021081073. Its “Adult Kidney Stem Cells” section reports no evidence of new nephron generation within a postnatal mammalian kidney, including after injury. This concerns nephron formation within the native kidney; it does not exclude formation of mammalian nephron tissue in engineered or transplanted settings.

The review describes tubular epithelial repair, experimental reprogramming toward nephron progenitor states, and vascularized human stem cell-derived kidney tissue in animal recipients. These are relevant component achievements, but they do not demonstrate clinically meaningful addition of new, urine-draining nephrons within an adult human’s native kidney. Kidney organoids discussed in the review resemble first- to second-trimester fetal kidney tissue rather than a mature postnatal organ. Their multicellular organization and transcriptional resemblance to developing kidney therefore do not establish adult renal replacement function.

In situ regeneration remains a prospective approach in that review. No supplied human study demonstrates the target capability. The evidence package contains no freshness search record establishing developments after the review, so it cannot determine whether the capability remained undemonstrated as of November 1, 2026. Retrieval of the review on that date does not update its scientific coverage. Feasibility in people remains uncertain on the supplied evidence.

Evidence access: the supplied validated review reports access to the full retained HTML text, including the body, conclusion, and references, without reported truncation. Its relevant scientific findings were explicit in the prose; figure images were not supplied or inspected. The earlier research’s description of indexed-only access is therefore superseded for this assessment. This record relies on that supplied assessment and does not represent a new inspection of the source.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing biological demonstration: establish that treatment creates additional whole nephrons inside an adult human’s native kidney, with functional vascular connections and drainage into the collecting system. The evidence should distinguish new nephron formation from repair, enlargement, or improved performance of existing nephrons, and should connect the added structures to a sustained improvement in measured renal function. The review supports the importance of quantity, perfusion, and drainage; the demonstration proposed here extends those requirements to native-kidney regeneration.
completion_criteria.label: Additional integrated nephrons sustain function in native human kidneys

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: in adults with substantially reduced kidney function, show enough sustained recovery to avoid or stop dialysis for a clearly defined group, without transplantation of a replacement organ, and maintain the benefit for years. Dialysis decisions should reflect adequate overall renal function rather than a filtration measurement in isolation. Dialysis avoidance or cessation and multiyear durability are demanding thresholds proposed for this concept, not established standards endorsed by the supplied review.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained renal recovery avoids or stops dialysis for years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the anatomical and functional findings in independent studies, define the patient population and disease conditions in which benefit occurs, and monitor whether regeneration disrupts existing function or produces abnormal tissue. A protocol should specify how new nephron number, causal contribution to function, safety, and durability will be assessed. Success in a finite set of patients or kidney diseases would establish that demonstrated breadth, without proving applicability to every cause or stage of kidney failure.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce nephron regeneration and establish clinical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed exclusions: tubular repair biomarkers, nephron-like structures without functional integration, or a temporary filtration increase without evidence of additional nephrons would not establish this capability. Earlier demonstrations of safe, integrated nephron addition could constitute substantial progress even before reaching the proposed dialysis and multiyear clinical thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Integrated nephron addition distinguished from repair or temporary filtration gains

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CLM-05, “Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale,” and CLM-11, “Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body,” address organ replacement. CLM-15 addresses increasing nephron number within the patient’s existing kidney. Stem cell differentiation, tissue organization, vascular integration, and urinary drainage may overlap technically with CLM-11, but an implanted engineered kidney would not itself demonstrate native-kidney nephron regeneration. Likewise, implantation of a pig kidney belongs to CLM-05 even if it restores renal function.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-04, “Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury,” and CLM-06, “Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart,” share the ambition of restoring function through tissue reconstruction. They remain distinct because successful nephron generation does not establish neural circuit reconnection or production of functional heart muscle. Adult limb regeneration is not a separate entry in the supplied roster.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-08, “Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging,” and CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver,” could overlap with CLM-15 through reprogramming or delivery technologies. Such overlap is conditional: restoring nephron number need not reverse aging across tissues or require genome writing, and neither of those capabilities alone establishes formation of complete integrated nephrons.

At the treatment-mechanism level, tubular repair and therapies that slow fibrosis can preserve or improve kidney function without increasing whole-nephron number. They are relevant complementary approaches, while CLM-15 requires evidence of additional nephrons. The review’s distinction between repair of a damaged organ and replacement using engineered tissue helps explain why these approaches can share clinical goals while requiring different demonstrations.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish developments after the January 2022 review or the field’s status as of November 1, 2026.
The cell source and induction strategy capable of safely producing complete new nephrons within an adult human’s native kidney remain unspecified.
The number, maturity, and performance of added nephrons needed for meaningful clinical benefit or dialysis independence remain unresolved.
A clinical protocol still needs methods for establishing new nephron formation, functional drainage, and the causal contribution of added nephrons to renal recovery.
Durability, safety, and effectiveness across different causes and stages of kidney disease remain to be demonstrated.

brief.title: Growing new filtering units in adult kidneys
possible: People with damaged kidneys could regain working capacity within their own organs. Treatment would add nephrons, the microscopic units that filter blood and turn the filtered fluid into urine. Each new unit would connect to blood vessels and the kidney’s urine drainage system.
why: Replacing lost nephrons could restore kidney capacity beyond what repairing surviving cells can achieve. Enough lasting recovery could let some people avoid or stop dialysis, a treatment that replaces part of the kidneys’ work, without needing a donor kidney.

sources.who: Melissa H. Little and Benjamin D. Humphreys
sources.showed: Their review described repair of existing kidney cells and progress in growing kidney tissue. It reported no evidence that mammals form new nephrons within their own kidneys after birth.
sources.quote: What is clear is that there is no evidence in any mammalian species of an ability to generate new nephrons in a postnatal kidney, with or without an injury trigger.
sources.cited_for: The review explains the biological gap between kidney repair and adding whole nephrons.
sources.not_established: It establishes no treatment that adds working nephrons within an adult human’s own kidney.

sources.who: The authors of the pig-kidney transplantation study
sources.showed: Researchers grew kidney organoids, small lab-grown tissues resembling developing kidneys, and delivered them into pig kidneys kept functioning outside the body. Human cells persisted after the kidneys were returned to the pigs.
sources.quote: We infuse human kidney organoids into ex vivo porcine kidneys using normothermic machine perfusion, and demonstrate in vivo engraftment of hPSC-kidney organoids.
sources.cited_for: Human kidney tissue can be delivered into pig kidneys and survive reimplantation.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish added nephrons that filter blood, drain urine and durably improve an adult human kidney’s function.

sources.who: Sun Ah Nam, Eunjeong Seo and collaborators
sources.showed: Human kidney organoids transplanted into mice survived for months and gained blood vessels from their hosts. They remained immature and developed cysts, cartilage and expanding supporting tissue.
sources.quote: Kidney organoid grafts survived for months after transplantation and became vascularized from host mouse endothelial cells.
sources.cited_for: Transplanted kidney tissue can acquire blood vessels while retaining problems with maturity and abnormal growth.
sources.not_established: Blood vessel growth alone does not establish safe, mature nephrons that drain urine and restore kidney function.

shown: Researchers have grown human kidney organoids and transplanted them into animal kidneys. The pig-kidney study found human cells after reimplantation. Nam, Seo and collaborators showed that grafts in mice survived for months and acquired blood vessels, but remained immature and developed abnormal tissue.
missing: A treatment has yet to add complete, working nephrons inside an adult human’s own kidney, with blood flow and urine drainage.
Added nephrons have yet to deliver lasting recovery sufficient to avoid or stop dialysis.
Regeneration has yet to be controlled safely in diseased kidneys while preserving their remaining function.

milestones.label: New connected nephrons sustain human kidney function
milestones.explanation: Treatment would have to add whole nephrons inside an adult human’s own kidney, with blood flow, urine drainage and sustained functional gains. This would establish working additions to the organ.

milestones.label: Kidney recovery keeps people off dialysis for years
milestones.explanation: Adults with severely reduced kidney function would have to recover enough to avoid or stop dialysis for years without a replacement organ. This would establish a lasting clinical benefit.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce benefits and define who benefits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce new nephron formation and functional gains, define which patients benefit and track abnormal growth or damage. This would establish reproducibility and treatment boundaries.

milestones.label: Tests distinguish nephron addition from repair and temporary gains
milestones.explanation: Evidence would have to distinguish integrated new nephrons from repaired or enlarged existing units and temporary filtration gains. This would establish that added nephrons cause the recovery.

uncertain: Which cells or biological signals could safely produce complete new nephrons inside an adult kidney?
How many added nephrons, at what maturity and performance, would provide meaningful recovery?
How should studies prove that new nephrons drain urine and cause lasting recovery across different kidney diseases?

page.title: Nephron regeneration in the adult human kidney
page.definition: An adult human’s native kidney gains additional nephrons, the microscopic units that filter blood and modify filtrate into urine. The new units receive blood, perform filtration and tubular transport, drain into the kidney’s collecting system and increase kidney function.

goal.need: In 2023, 831,192 people in the United States lived with treated kidney failure. Of these, 67% received dialysis and 33% had a kidney transplant. Dialysis replaces only part of kidney function, and patients can wait years for a donor kidney. Surviving cells can repair damage within a nephron. When a whole nephron is lost, forming another would give the kidney an additional unit for filtration and tubular transport. If enough function were restored, people with progressive kidney disease could postpone dialysis or transplantation.

completion.title: Additional functioning nephrons increase the capacity of an adult human’s native kidney.
completion.criterion: A human study demonstrates an increase in the number of whole nephrons within adult native kidneys following an intervention. The added nephrons have perfused glomeruli that filter blood, tubules that process filtrate, and open connections to the native collecting system. The study demonstrates an increase in kidney function attributable to the added units.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback derived from NIDDK’s nephron-generation objective and published requirements for functional nephron integration.
completion.basis: Searches of NIDDK RBK calls, KHI roadmaps, KidneyX prize criteria and ClinicalTrials.gov-indexed protocols found no adult-human completion standard combining nephron addition, integration and functional benefit. The Atlas test applies the published nephron-generation, perfusion and urinary-drainage requirements to adult native human kidneys.

milestones.title: Human stem cells form segmented nephron structures in culture.
milestones.criterion: Human pluripotent stem cells form nephron structures in culture with a recognisable glomerular compartment and distinct proximal and distal tubular segments.
milestones.set_by: California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, grant LA1-06536, public abstract. The grant identifies human nephron cultures as the translation target for its mouse stem-cell work.

milestones.title: Implanted nephron tissue receives blood flow sufficient to sustain physiological function.
milestones.criterion: Host blood vessels perfuse implanted nephron tissue, and the perfused tissue remains viable and performs a physiological function such as glomerular filtration.
milestones.set_by: Kidney Health Initiative, Technology Roadmap research activities, cellular-product engraftment and perfusion objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrate perfusion of implanted tissue that is sufficient to maintain cell health and physiological functions

milestones.title: New nephron tissue drains filtrate into the host kidney’s collecting system.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate passage of filtrate from the new nephron tissue through an open connection into the host kidney’s collecting system.
milestones.set_by: NIDDK’s published account of the (Re)Building a Kidney presentation to its Advisory Council on 7 September 2018. Patent urinary outflow is also a published requirement for transplanted nephron tissue.
milestones.threshold_quote: the interconnection of the nephrons to the host collecting system.

milestones.title: Additional nephrons restore kidney function in an adult mammalian disease model.
milestones.criterion: In an adult mammalian model of kidney injury or disease, demonstrate an increase in whole-nephron number in the affected kidney and show that the added nephrons contribute to recovery of kidney function.
milestones.set_by: NIDDK, (Re)Building a Kidney funding call. The milestone applies the programme’s nephron-number and functional recovery objectives to an adult mammalian model.
milestones.threshold_quote: Evaluate the ability of these principles to restore kidney function in models of kidney injuries or diseases.

milestones.title: Adults receive an investigational nephron-regeneration treatment in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: Adults receive an investigational intervention in a phase 1 clinical study whose protocol identifies the addition of whole nephrons in their native kidneys as the intended effect.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a), for the phase 1 definition. Section 312.120 sets conditions for FDA acceptance of foreign studies conducted without a US investigational new drug application.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: Implanted nephron tubules secrete a waste solute into the tubular lumen in vivo.
milestones.criterion: In a living recipient, demonstrate that the implanted tubules contribute to removal of a waste solute by transporting it from the blood side of the tubular epithelium into the lumen. The measurement distinguishes tubular secretion from delivery of the solute by glomerular filtration.
milestones.set_by: Kidney Health Initiative, Technology Roadmap, toxin removal and secretion objective for implanted cell-based systems.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate toxin removal and secretory functionality of implanted cell-based systems in vivo

not_found: The searched programme documents and prize criteria supplied no numerical nephron-addition or durability threshold for adult human native-kidney regeneration.
No located human study established additional whole nephrons with filtration, tubular processing, native urinary drainage and attributable functional benefit.
ClinicalTrials.gov-indexed searches yielded no protocol testing that combined endpoint, and the direct registry search could not be opened.
The supplied 2022 review’s PMC page returned a browser challenge when reopened.
The kidney-replacement roadmap published on 6 November 2026 was subscription-limited beyond its abstract, key points and figure captions.
No position statement was found from a kidney society or funding programme concluding that adding functional nephrons to adult native kidneys is infeasible or unworthy of pursuit.

results.finding: NSG mice with nephron grafts (n = 6/group) had urinary uromodulin of 1188 ± 199.20 pg/mL.
results.detail: The urine assay measured the end product and could not resolve how the protein entered urine.
results.quote:

and UMOD (1188 ± 199.20 pg ml−1)i nt h ee n g r a f t e dm i c ec o m p a r e dt o
control mice with acellular scaffolds (Fig.7d and Supplementary Fig. S7a,b).

results.finding: NSG mice with nephron grafts (n = 6/group) had 72.74 ± 13.70 pg/mL human CD59 in urine.
results.detail: The authors identified diffusion and active tubular flow as possible routes for the urinary proteins.
results.quote:
Human protein CD59 was detected at a signiﬁcantly higher level in the
urine of engrafted mice on day (d) 21 (engraftment) in comparison to mice
implanted with an acellular scaffold (control) or healthy mice urine (healthy),
(n = 6 mouse per group from three independent biological replicates).

results.finding: Porcine kidney scaffolds (CT n = 3) showed contrast enhancement from 10 seconds after intravenous injection.
results.detail: Contrast enhancement measured blood delivery into the matrix. The authors inferred possible filtration from glomerular structure and contrast kinetics.
results.quote: Angiography and dynamic CT allowed imaging active blood flow in a part of the implanted matrix.

results.finding: Porcine kidney scaffolds showed weak urographic contrast enhancement at 28 days (urography sample size unspecified).
results.detail: Contrast was introduced from the ureter. The imaging did not establish that filtrate produced in the scaffold reached the host collecting system.
results.quote: An influx of a contrast agent inside the matrix was also observed using urography.

results.finding: Porcine kidney scaffolds contained glomerular and tubular structures at 28 days (regional glomerular counts n = 3).
results.detail: Regional histology counted glomerular structures. The study did not enumerate whole nephrons or measure functional recovery.
results.quote: Twenty-eight days after implantation, glomeruli, vessels, and renal tubules, characteristic of nephrons, were histologically observed within the matrix.

results.finding: Selected renal cell injections stabilized kidney disease progression in 2 rat models (5/6 nephrectomy, n=3; ZSF1, n=7).
results.detail: The sponsor reports changes in glomerular filtration, tubular protein handling, electrolyte balance and urine concentration. These measures do not establish the formation of additional whole nephrons.
results.quote:
This intervention strategy elicited a regenerative response that significantly improved survival 
and stabilized disease progression to renal structure and function, and extended the longevity in 
both the 5/6th Nx model and the ZSF1 model of CKD.

results.finding: Seven adults with chronic kidney disease received Neo-Kidney Augment in a native kidney across two phase 1 studies.
results.detail: The phase II protocol reports prior phase 1 dosing and interim findings from the sponsor.
results.quote: To date, 7 patients have been biopsied and injected safely with NKA.

results.finding: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived kidney organoids formed glomerular, proximal and distal nephron compartments by day 14 in culture (imaging sample size unspecified).
results.detail: Figure 3B–C identifies the compartments by morphology and marker staining. Single-cell RNA sequencing corroborates the segment identities.
results.quote:
By day 14, they developed into larger and more elaborated and segmented nephrons with NPHS1/PODXL
+
podocyte (pod)-containing glomeruli, LRP2
+
proximal tubules (PT), SLC12A1
+
thick ascending limb (TAL), and a short GATA3
+
connecting segment (CNT) that fused to CDs.

results.finding: Embryonic kidney grafts in adult anephric rats (cohort n=5) achieved approximately 15% of healthy-control creatinine clearance.
results.detail: The text gives the cohort size but leaves the exact sample size for each clearance time point unspecified. Tubular secretion can cause creatinine clearance to overestimate glomerular filtration.
results.quote: and creatinine clearance, an indicator of glomerular filtration rate, was approximately 15%

results.finding: Integrated embryonic kidney grafts in adult rats achieved an 83.3% urinary tract connection success rate (n=12).
results.detail: The graft bladder was surgically connected to the ureter of the removed left kidney.
results.quote: The success rate of urinary tract connection improved from 66.7% (6 of 9) with single MNBs to 83.3% (10 of 12) with integrated MNB grafts, likely due to increased urine accumulation in the fused bladders

results.finding: In adult wild-type zebrafish, 10 of 12 regenerated nephron tubules were positive for fluorescent dextran.
results.detail: The assay scored dextran-containing vesicles on the apical or lumenal side of newly formed tubules. Passage across the junction was inferred from tracer uptake and lumen continuity.
results.quote: In wild type, EdU +  new tubules were also positive for dextran ( Fig. 7J ; 10/12 tubules; 83%), indicating fluid flow and successful connections had been established.

goal.need = "In 2023, 831,192 people in the United States lived with treated kidney failure. Of these, 67% received dialysis and 33% had a kidney transplant. Dialysis replaces only part of kidney function, and patients can wait years for a donor kidney. Surviving cells can repair damage within a nephron. When a whole nephron is lost, forming another would give the kidney an additional unit for filtration and tubular transport. If enough function were restored, people with progressive kidney disease could postpone dialysis or transplantation.". Reason: The existing rationale gives an older count and leaves out the patient benefit, the limits of dialysis and the distinction between repairing a nephron and replacing one.

add statement by National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, 2019: "test novel ways to increase nephron number or nephron function.". Reason: The 2019 funding call explicitly identifies increasing nephron number as an objective of in vivo regeneration.

edit m1: criterion = "Human pluripotent stem cells form nephron structures in culture with a recognisable glomerular compartment and distinct proximal and distal tubular segments."; set_by = "California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, grant LA1-06536, public abstract. The grant identifies human nephron cultures as the translation target for its mouse stem-cell work."; threshold_quote = "translation of de novo nephrogenesis to human nephron cultures"; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7, 21, 8]. Reason: The culture criterion includes mouse transplantation schedules and graft complications that do not determine whether human cells formed segmented nephrons in culture.

edit m2: criterion = "Host blood vessels perfuse implanted nephron tissue, and the perfused tissue remains viable and performs a physiological function such as glomerular filtration."; threshold_quote = "demonstrate perfusion of implanted tissue that is sufficient to maintain cell health and physiological functions"; threshold_ref = 9. Reason: The tracer sizes, observation times and percentage of filtering glomeruli are results from one experiment rather than thresholds set by the roadmap.

add milestone after m2: "Implanted nephron tubules secrete a waste solute into the tubular lumen in vivo.". Reason: The roadmap gives tubular secretion its own in vivo test because glomerular filtration alone cannot establish that a tubule moves solutes from blood into filtrate.

edit m3: criterion = "Demonstrate passage of filtrate from the new nephron tissue through an open connection into the host kidney\u2019s collecting system."; threshold_quote = "the interconnection of the nephrons to the host collecting system."; threshold_ref = 11. Reason: The cited experiment shows fusion within a graft, whereas this milestone requires filtrate to cross into the host collecting system.

edit m4: criterion = "In an adult mammalian model of kidney injury or disease, demonstrate an increase in whole-nephron number in the affected kidney and show that the added nephrons contribute to recovery of kidney function."; set_by = "NIDDK, (Re)Building a Kidney funding call. The milestone applies the programme\u2019s nephron-number and functional recovery objectives to an adult mammalian model."; threshold_quote = "Evaluate the ability of these principles to restore kidney function in models of kidney injuries or diseases."; threshold_ref = 6. Reason: The current criterion mixes a test of whole-kidney function with observations of tissue structures and leaves unclear which model conditions come from the programme.

edit m5: criterion = "Adults receive an investigational intervention in a phase 1 clinical study whose protocol identifies the addition of whole nephrons in their native kidneys as the intended effect."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a), for the phase 1 definition. Section 312.120 sets conditions for FDA acceptance of foreign studies conducted without a US investigational new drug application."; threshold_quote = "Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans."; threshold_ref = 15; refs = [15, 22]. Reason: The current wording requires direct administration into the kidney and a US investigational new drug application even though the phase 1 definition specifies neither route nor a universal US filing requirement.
